analysis.one_liner: Requires mortgage servicers to try mediation and offer loan modifications before foreclosing.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee in December 2011, referred to a subcommittee in January 2012, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped mortgage servicers from starting a foreclosure unless they first made a real effort to set up a mediation session — a meeting run under Department of Housing and Urban Development rules to determine whether the homeowner qualifies for a loan modification or another alternative like a short sale. It would also have suspended foreclosure actions already underway until mediation was completed, and made a violation a bar to the foreclosure itself. A servicer could avoid the suspension only by documenting that the homeowner declined mediation.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners in default or at risk of falling behind on their mortgages. The bill gave them a guaranteed chance to sit down with the servicer and determine whether their loan could be modified or resolved through an alternative to foreclosure, rather than losing the house through a foreclosure filed without any such step.

how_it_helps.text: A servicer could not initiate a foreclosure until it made a reasonable effort to start mediation and, if the borrower was eligible, offered a loan modification or an alternative to foreclosure such as a short sale or deed in lieu [S2] [S3].

Foreclosure actions already underway when the bill became law would have been suspended until mediation was completed, and during that suspension the servicer could not send a foreclosure notice, schedule or conduct a sale of the property, or allow a final judgment against the borrower [S2] [S3].
A servicer that violated the requirements would be barred from the foreclosure action until it came into compliance [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage servicers, who would have had to pause foreclosures, participate in mediation, and report quarterly to HUD on their mediation efforts, and the investors holding the mortgage pools behind them, who could face longer timelines and larger write-downs when modifications reduced what borrowers owed.

drawbacks.text: The bill let a servicer escape the suspension requirement simply by documenting that it made a reasonable effort to schedule mediation and the borrower did not agree to one, so a homeowner who ignored the outreach could lose that protection [S2] [S3].

It also stated that nothing in the bill would require a servicer to delay an 'unavoidable' foreclosure, such as one involving an abandoned property, and that once a servicer came into compliance it could proceed with the foreclosure regardless of any prior violation — meaning the process added steps and delay but did not guarantee any homeowner kept a home [S2] [S3].

Suspension periods, mediation, and quarterly reporting would add costs and time for servicers and mortgage investors, which critics could reasonably argue would raise servicing costs across the market [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection — no foreclosure filing without a documented attempt at mediation and an offer of modification if the borrower qualifies — was a meaningful safeguard during a period when foreclosure volumes were still high after the housing crash, and the carve-outs for borrowers who refused mediation and for abandoned properties limited the risk of abuse. The bill would not have saved every home, but it put the burden on servicers to prove they explored alternatives before taking a house. The main cost fell on servicers and investors in the form of delay and potential write-downs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Financial Services Committee and its housing subcommittee without ever getting a hearing or a vote, and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Frederica Wilson of Florida introduced the bill on December 7, 2011, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1] [S5].
On January 12, 2012, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Insurance, Housing and Community Opportunity, and no further action appears in the record [S5].
The bill had 2 Democratic cosponsors and never advanced past subcommittee referral before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage servicers and mortgage investors are better off because the bill never advanced: they avoided a federal requirement to suspend foreclosures and complete mediation before filing or continuing a foreclosure.

for.name: Rep. Frederica Wilson
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Mandatory Foreclosure Mediation Act on December 7, 2011.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over housing and mortgage servicing
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: Subcommittee on Insurance, Housing and Community Opportunity
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 12, 2012 and took no action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican support appears in the record, and the Republican-led Financial Services Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: Servicers would have had to complete mediation and offer eligible borrowers a modification or alternative before filing or continuing a foreclosure, and to report quarterly to HUD. That pauses foreclosure timelines and can force write-downs, so servicers' interest in the status quo ran against homeowners seeking to keep their homes.

Investors in mortgage pools could see longer timelines and larger losses when principal-reducing modifications were offered, but they also avoid the added costs of vacant, foreclosed properties in some cases. The bill's definition of servicer explicitly includes those responsible for servicing pools of mortgages.

industries.industry: HUD-approved mediation and housing counseling providers
industries.note: A HUD-established mandatory mediation process would have created a nationwide demand for mediation proceedings and servicer reporting. Their interest runs alongside homeowners seeking a face-to-face review.
